items.title: Prioritise, categorise and share To Do list
items.summary: I'm looking for a way of creating a To Do list. There are 4 of us in my team and each person will have a list of tasks. I want to set a priority and category to each task and have each assigned to one of us. I'd like to be able to see all tasks in a single list and also be able to filter them by team member, priority and category. Ideally, I'd like to be able to add notes in an individual task. I could do it in Excel but wondered if there is any software that does it out of the box. Also, I work for the health service and paid software won't be an option unfortunately. Thanks.

deep.body: I'm looking for a way of creating a To Do list. There are 4 of us in my team and each person will have a list of tasks. I want to set a priority and category to each task and have each assigned to one of us. I'd like to be able to see all tasks in a single list and also be able to filter them by team member, priority and category. Ideally, I'd like to be able to add notes in an individual task. I could do it in Excel but wondered if there is any software that does it out of the box. Also, I work for the health service and paid software won't be an option unfortunately. Thanks.

comments.text: Maybe this points you in good direction: Kanban is a visual workflow management method that optimizes processes by displaying tasks on a board. This helps teams track work progress efficiently, typically using columns like "Todo," "In Progress," "Done," and "QA". But you could also do this with a single column layout where you only have a "Todo" column. Online Kanban tools offer features such as assignments, labels, notes, and comments. So finding a Kanban tool with your requirements should not be to hard. Finding a free HIPAA-Compliant Kanban board might be challenging, but there are open-source options available for self-hosting.

If your organisation is on Microsoft 365 (most NHS and other health-service organisations are, via NHSmail), Microsoft Planner does all of this at no extra cost: One plan for the team , with each of the four of you added as members. Category: use buckets (columns) or labels for the categories. Priority: every task has a priority field (Urgent / Important / Medium / Low). Assigned to: each task can be assigned to one or more people. Notes: each task has a notes field, a checklist and comments. Single list + filters: the Grid view shows every task in one list, and the Filter button narrows it by assignee, priority, label or due date. Group by "Assigned to" gives each person's list. It also appears inside Teams (add Planner as a tab in your team's channel), so nobody needs another login.

items.title: Open-source Google Keep alternatives?
items.summary: Is there any comparable alternative to Google's Keep? Features I require: notes must support including images (via copy and paste) and other files (PDFs) and treat them as attachments/image gallery, not necessarily inline (because there may be many images/large images) notes, images and PDFs must be indexed/searchable (via OCR (ie easyocr)) I wrote a note taking app with integrated live search ( https://github.com/jjYBdx4IL/ajax-solnotes ), but abandoned it because Google Keep does perfect OCR on images, which I can just copy and paste into notes there.

deep.body: Is there any comparable alternative to Google's Keep? Features I require: notes must support including images (via copy and paste) and other files (PDFs) and treat them as attachments/image gallery, not necessarily inline (because there may be many images/large images) notes, images and PDFs must be indexed/searchable (via OCR (ie easyocr)) I wrote a note taking app with integrated live search ( https://github.com/jjYBdx4IL/ajax-solnotes ), but abandoned it because Google Keep does perfect OCR on images, which I can just copy and paste into notes there. I also don't really want to create a new fancy UI from scratch. So what would you recommend to achieve the goal? Is there a universal UI framework that let's me build that without re-inventing the UI wheel? Or is there a complete and free solution already existing that I simply overlooked?

comments.text: Check out Obsidian . It is available for PC (Windows, Linux, Mac) and mobile platforms (Android, iOS). All files are stored locally in Markdown format. It has many plugins that extend its capabilities, including OCR .

Joplin is the closest open-source fit for your two requirements: Attachments: you can paste images straight into a note and attach PDFs and other files; they are stored as resources of the note rather than having to be inline. OCR search: since Joplin 3.0 the desktop app can run OCR (Tesseract) on image and PDF attachments, and the recognised text is included in search. It is off by default; switch it on in the settings. It is free (AGPL), has apps for Windows, macOS, Linux, Android and iOS, and you pick the sync target (Nextcloud, WebDAV, Dropbox, OneDrive, or a self-hosted Joplin Server), so nothing has to leave your own infrastructure. One caveat: OCR runs in the desktop app, so images pasted on the phone become searchable once a desktop client has synced and processed them.

items.title: GUI for editing multiple JSON files
items.summary: I am looking to edit JSON files in bulk / batch. I know I can do this programmatically, or do find/replaces across files, but I am hoping to find a friendlier GUI that allows me to do things across a selection of files like: editing a certain key: adding a key nice to have: seeing stats of the value of a specific key to quickly spot typo's Is there something available like this for any OS, or as a webapp?

deep.body: I am looking to edit JSON files in bulk / batch. I know I can do this programmatically, or do find/replaces across files, but I am hoping to find a friendlier GUI that allows me to do things across a selection of files like: editing a certain key: adding a key nice to have: seeing stats of the value of a specific key to quickly spot typo's Is there something available like this for any OS, or as a webapp? To clarify what I mean, I have included two example json files below: File 1: { "title": "Some title", "categories": [ "Category 1", "Category 2" ], "specs": [ "Up", "Down", "Left", 43 ], "price: { "type": "Upper", "amount": 5, }, "delivery: { "type": "Pickup", "amount": 1, }, } File 2: { "title": "Some other title", "categories": [ "Category 1", "Catergoy 6" ], "specs": [ "Up", 42 ], "price: { "type": "Upper", "amount": 6, }, "delivery: { "type": "Address", "amount": 2, }, "status": sold } I am looking for GUI software that would allow me to e.g.: edit the price.amount key and set it to 10 for all selected files add a key status to all files, choosing whether or not I want to overwrite any existing keys show all values for the key category , such that I can quickly see that there are 3 distinct values of which one has a typo ( Categroy 6 ).

comments.text: Various text editors allow you to open several files at once and do find and replace over several. I use Notepad++. Your question is a little vague. Any software that would allow more then find and replace would be so complex to use that you might as well write a script for it. Batch replace with Notepad++ is explained in this SO answer .
Check out Kate (from KDE). The application is cross-platform and very functional. But for mass editing of JSON values, it is probably better to write a simple Python script.

items.title: Where do you see Software in 5 years?
items.summary: I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next. For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp. I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software. That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs?

deep.body: I wanted to hear some good opinions on all things AI and how they transform the Software industry. I'm anxious about the future and lack the foresight to form any opinion on what to do next. For context, I'm a L4 SWE that has more or less say 5-10 yrs of exp. I've enjoyed my work throughout my career, AI makes me ship more, much more than I could do 3 years ago. I feel I use it well and it translates into really good software. That said, what do you think happens in years to come with the Software industry in general? Do you think we'll go through a massive erosion of jobs? What's your perspective on that? I'm asking because I honestly don't know what to do: I can try to always keep up to date with newest technologies, best practices, but I'm only me; if the demand for SWEs and jobs falls to the floor, I'm not sure I'll always get a place at the table (i.e. land a job) and I'm wondering whether I should try to do something else in some other industry. It feels weird to be in a good position in life and still constantly worry about it getting worse.

comments.text: where do you see it in 5 years? if you're anxious about job security, standing out in your career is generally not specific to the industry you are in.

In 5 years time software will exist in 3 silos. It's really not any different today, except the talent will continue to diverge. Silo 1 - This will be employers strongly forcing AI for most task completion. This will be most large corporate employers and most start ups. There will be little to no working knowledge of the internals of large applications and these employers will bleed money on outside consultants to occasionally provide manual maintenance and security hot fixes. Everything will continue to look good from the outside, but really its a messy house of cards. Silo 2 - This will be institutional shops of skilled experts. Game companies that own internally developed rendering engines, kernel developers, independent open source, and systems architects come to mind. These will be people that might occasionally dabble in AI for various things, but they manually modify their code.
In 5 years I don't see myself using any software that I didn't design and build myself. I'm already ~30-40% there, 100% is not yet feasible but in 5 years time (maybe less) it will happen.

Software as we know it will be gone in 5 years. AI will have replaced all our existing software, using new languages, new AI created frameworks completely foreign to our current approaches and installed base of systems and application software. In 5 years We will have far passed the ability and need to review code. We will have phenomenal AI reviews to do that. Existing tools, systems, frameworks and such just won't matter, would just slow down AI. Replacing complete vertical system silos will be done in a single, crazy step, efficient to run, secured by an awesome security AI. I recently retired after working in software development from 1975 to 2025 encompassing punch cards to AI.

To me it never changed, I like coding because for the sake of it and i like learning, AI came and i adapted, i didn't expect it to grow this fast and change software landscape this much. But i was there when gpt2 and 3 came out i even had early access and I learned how it worked and I can say one thing companies still need software engineers as long as LLMs themselves exists, this isn't end all and be all they are trying to force this idea into existence AI by this time should have already replaced all coders but it isn't because giant corporations are trying to force scaling instead of finding a way to make them more intelligent in a meaningful way.

Everyone wants a crystal ball on where this will end up. Reality is none of us have any idea - there's a risk to any decision you make. I can make a decent sounding argument for any side. The onramp for coding becoming easier means non-tech people finally have a cheaper way to try out business ideas for domains they're experts in. Many of those will succeed and will need to hire developers, massively increasing the demand. Coding becoming easier means many more people will jump in, reducing wages rapidly. While there might be some work available, it'll mostly be low paid. Now that one person can do the job of 5, 4/5 will be laid off and we'll all struggle to get work. Now that one person can do the job of 5, AND there will be an increased demand for more developers from more businesses popping up, we'll be paid a hell of a lot more for the value we can generate.

items.title: GitLab 19.6.0 is out and still vulnerable to Ruby2Shell and NGINX2Root
items.summary: What's going on at GitLab? They released their usual monthly release 19.6.0 to their package repos (https://packages.gitlab.com/gitlab/gitlab-ee/ubuntu/jammy/pool/main/g/gitlab-ee/) but did not announce it at all as of 3.5h after release (https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/all-releases.xml, https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/19/gitlab-19-6-released/). But more annoyingly, this release does not address ruby2shell or nginx2root, nor do patches for their older releases exist yet and there's no communication on any of this (that I can find).

deep.body: What's going on at GitLab? They released their usual monthly release 19.6.0 to their package repos (https://packages.gitlab.com/gitlab/gitlab-ee/ubuntu/jammy/pool/main/g/gitlab-ee/) but did not announce it at all as of 3.5h after release (https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/all-releases.xml, https://docs.gitlab.com/releases/19/gitlab-19-6-released/). But more annoyingly, this release does not address ruby2shell or nginx2root, nor do patches for their older releases exist yet and there's no communication on any of this (that I can find). root@gitlab:~# cat /opt/gitlab/embedded/service/gitlab-rails/VERSION 19.6.0-ee root@gitlab:~# /opt/gitlab/embedded/sbin/nginx -version nginx version: nginx/1.31.7 root@gitlab:~# /opt/gitlab/embedded/bin/ruby --version ruby 3.3.13 (2026-10-23 revision af48f08f21) [x86_64-linux] root@gitlab:~# lsb_release -a No LSB modules are available. Distributor ID: Ubuntu Description: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS Release: 22.04 Codename: jammy Multiple MRs were created in their repos 14-15 hours ago, no urgency visible. Heres 2 I found: https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/omnibus-gitlab/-/merge_requests/10138 https://gitlab.com/gitlab-org/omnibus-gitlab/-/merge_requests/10139

comments.text: "Application security: Taking days when minutes matter" --Software mantra for 2026.
too many 2shell these days
is this only for self hosted?

The pre-release info on 19.6.0 says that it addresses nginx2shell: https://docs.gitlab.com/update/versions/gitlab_19_changes/#n... There is also a workaround to disable http2 from NGINX and make that part safe. I'm leaving HTTP2 disabled for the forseeable future. - edit /etc/gitlab/gitlab.rb - add lines: gitlab_rails['nginx']['http2_enabled'] = false nginx['http2_enabled'] = false - save and run: gitlab-ctl reconfigure - finally run: gitlab-ctl restart nginx There is no workaorund for Ruby2Shell though :( As it was just dropped last night, well after they would have started testing etc for 19.6.0, it's no surprise it's not in there. Also, since they konw 19.6.0 has Ruby2Shell in it, it's not much surprise they haven't been promoting it, or that they are scrambling. GitLab is such a huge beast that it can't be quick to get changes made and run through tests for everything.

items.summary: Hey HN, we’re Nel and Kosi. We noticed personal agents like Instinct, Muse were terrible at buying stuff. Most of the time the checkout would fail. So we built reliable automations for agents to checkout at 9 leading grocery merchants. We grapple with anti bot, logins, OTP codes, and changing checkout structures. Loved revisiting this stuff given our backgrounds sneaker-botting and building computer use models. Honestly full circle haha.

deep.body: Hey HN, we’re Nel and Kosi. We noticed personal agents like Instinct, Muse were terrible at buying stuff. Most of the time the checkout would fail. So we built reliable automations for agents to checkout at 9 leading grocery merchants. We grapple with anti bot, logins, OTP codes, and changing checkout structures. Loved revisiting this stuff given our backgrounds sneaker-botting and building computer use models. Honestly full circle haha. It currently works on these sites with ~70% checkout success rate: - Walmart - Albertsons - Ocado - Wegmans - FreshDirect - Best Buy - Instacart Our goal is to hill climb to 90%+ across each. Test keys are free and run the real flow without placing an order. New accounts get 10 free completed orders. https://docs.getagentmall.com/quickstart

items.title: Tool: Kiri
items.summary: Docker Desktop alternative. What we like: Single, Docker-compatible daemon (CLI, Compose, buildx). Performance optimized with a small memory footprint. Includes networks, volumes, k8s. Dev tools like auto-HTTPs endpoints with publicly sharable URLs. Supports macOS, Windows, Linux. What we dislike: Non-native UI, unlike something like Orbstack (which is macOS only). “Machines” are containers with filesystem access, not true VMs.

items.title: Tool: Jiff

Built-in handling of common date operations like durations, differences, calculations, geo regions. Uses Rust-native formatting and display options, including friendly formats. What we dislike: Shows you how complex dates and times actually are, but that probably means fewer bugs!
